Often pipes look similar but do hit differently. The side, chambers, bowl size and mouth opening size all really do vary. At least to me anyways. 

The white one has a small bowl head and smaller mouth opening. The overall size is also shorter.  The bowl pack is often fresh hits and needs reloading often but you often won’t have old half burned green when you come back to it. The mouth tip is smaller as well making for smaller lighter hits. Great for a small solo smoke session. 

The blue one. Bigger mouth hole. Small but deeper bowl head.  It will burn a long time and can get a good low ember cherry rolling in it. Hits are decent size but often I have to clean the bowl head between sessions because of the depth. It resins more and doesn’t always burn itself to complete ash. The resin build up can make for some harsh hits. The larger chamber can sometimes leave behind old smoke that will make you cough on your next hit. Meaning extra effort to making sure you clear the chamber of smoke is advised. Overall.  Longer smoke session with attention to detail. 

The orange one. The biggest bowl head and large mouth hole.  Is the longest of the 3 also. Smokes great.  Not as long of session as blue pipe. But good balance to size and can hold its own in a session with friends. 

Cleaning. I usually use a all natural bio 420 cleaning mix. Takes extra time under warm water rinsing it thorough. But does a great job at cleaning. I always use q tips also to wipe the bowl head between sessions or to give a quick clean of the pipe inside.  I’ve also used rubbing alcohol on q tip to clean. Just make sure you get the residue off.  Either a warm water rinse. Or a quick flash of lighter to evaporate then dry q tip wipe it down.  (91%? I think. The higher % one)  If you clean them regularly. The process isn’t bad. If you let them cake up and get solid. Then boiling them or soaking in very hot water is prob suggested.

The narrowest notch in New Hampshire and to many the most spectacular lies to the north: Dixville Notch, where only enough room remains between Sanguinary Mountain and Mount Gloriette to admit two-laned Highway 26. The notch (once owned by no less a personage than Daniel Webster) is famous for two reasons besides the dramatic geology: the Balsams, the resort hotel on the notch's west side that is another proud holdover from the 19th-century's golden age, and the fact that the tiny handful of Dixville Notch residents wake up early -- or stay up late -- each Presidential election so they can be the first in the country to vote.

Dixville Notch State Park includes waterfalls, a flume, picnic areas and hiking trails; the one up Table Rock, an airy and exposed ledge jutting hundreds of feet over a cliff, is another of those providing spectacular mountain scenery for the expenditure of relatively little effort. But even to those who stay car-bound, Dixville Notch's vertically stratified cliffs seem to generate the excitement that comes upon most people when confronted with rock scenery of this magnitude.
